doc.title: Jane Monheit interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, August 20, 2010

title: Being a jazz singer and widening genre
summary: Compared with Nancy Wilson, she accepts being a jazz singer while singing other styles; interpretation matters more than song choice.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: When I spoke with — I was lucky enough to get an interview with Nancy Wilson and she said that she just wanted to be known as “a singer.” She felt I guess that she’d been typecast as a jazz singer, but that’s not how she felt about herself. You on the other hand have said, “I’m a jazz singer.” So what makes that? Is it the repertoire you choose?

Well you know what, the definition of what makes a jazz singer now has loosened and expanded so completely. And you know what, I’m a lot of different kinds of singers. I mean there’s so much that I love to do. I mean I could call myself a jazz singer. I could call myself a musical theater singer because I can do that too. I could call myself a pop singer because I can do that too. It’s just that jazz is really the center. It’s what I really grew up doing and it’s what suits me the best and it’s what I do for a living. I mean I get up on stage with a jazz trio and I improvise and I sing standards, but I like to get outside it too, and we all do. We all do. I mean what was it, Ella recorded like “Sunshine of Your Love” I think.

You know, I think I’m getting that right. I mean Sarah Vaughan did all kinds of stuff. I mean everybody sings The Beatles. Everybody. I mean everybody has been just changing the definition of what that means. It’s less about the choice of your song now and more about how you interpret it.
